status_reasoning: The claim that undifferentiated H9 hESCs express only 6 TAFs (2,3,5,6,7,11) is supported by multiple independent methods: immunoblotting (Figure 1A), qRT-PCR (Figure 1B), and ChIP (Figure 4B). The convergence of orthogonal techniques strengthens confidence, though the authors acknowledge possible low-level expression below detection limits.

Retinoic acid-induced differentiation results in expression of all TAFs (previously absent TAFs 1,4,8,9,10,12,13 are induced) while maintaining expression of TAFs 2,3,5,6,7,11. This is well-documented by immunoblotting (Figure 1D) with appropriate positive (NES induction) and negative (OCT4 loss) differentiation controls.

The existence of a non-canonical TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex is supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation showing co-migration (Figure 2A) and co-immunoprecipitation demonstrating stable TBP association with TAFs 2,6,7,11 but not TAFs 3,5 (Figure 2B). The biochemical evidence is internally consistent and uses appropriate controls.

The two-class model of gene regulation (Class I: TAF3/5+TBP; Class II: all 6 TAFs+TBP) is supported by directed ChIP on 10 genes (Figures 3-4) and comparison with HeLa cells showing different TAF usage for the same genes. The model is mechanistically consistent with the biochemical complex data (R3).

Global ChIP-chip analysis confirms the two-class model genome-wide with high overlap between TAF3/5 (96.8%) and between TAF7/11 (81.5% by ChIP-chip, 92.3% by validation ChIP). Directed validation of 44 genes (Figure 7) shows higher co-occupancy than ChIP-chip predicted, suggesting the ChIP-chip may underestimate but the core finding is robust.

RNAi knockdown experiments functionally validate the two-class model: TAF3/5 depletion affects both class I and II genes (Figure 5A), while TAF2,6,7,11 depletion affects only class II genes (Figure 5B). This is the expected pattern if TAF3/5 are required for all active genes while TAF2,6,7,11 are specific to class II genes.

Knockdown of any of the six hESC TAFs causes loss of pluripotency markers (decreased alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies, NANOG downregulation) and induction of differentiation markers (Figure 8A-C). The consistency across all six TAFs and use of multiple differentiation markers provides strong evidence, though incomplete knockdown (acknowledged in C98) may complicate interpretation.

Ectopic expression of TAFs normally absent from hESCs (particularly TAF1) causes differentiation, loss of pluripotency markers, and selective downregulation of class II genes while sparing class I genes (Figure 8D-I). The ChIP data showing loss of TBP/POL2 recruitment to OCT4 promoter provides a mechanistic explanation. Controls showing no effect from ectopic TBP or endogenous TAFs strengthen the specificity.

The overarching conclusion that selective TAF expression/use underlies hESC self-renewal is supported by the convergence of loss-of-function (R7) and gain-of-function (R8) experiments, both showing that altering TAF composition disrupts pluripotency. However, this is a high-level interpretive claim that integrates multiple results.

Statistical analysis of ChIP-chip data reveals two significant differences between class I and II genes: class I promoters have higher H3K4me3 (p<10^-13) and class II genes more frequently have alternative promoters (p<10^-58) (Table 1, Figure 6E-F). The statistical significance is strong, though functional relevance of these differences remains unclear.

Immunoblot analysis clearly shows that mouse ESCs express TAFs 1,4,8,9,10,13 that are absent in human ESCs (Figure 9), demonstrating species-specific differences in TAF composition. This is a straightforward descriptive finding with appropriate controls.

The paper acknowledges ~12% mouse feeder cell contamination in ChIP samples and potential cell line differences (H9 vs H1). While the authors argue their H9 data is internally consistent and validated by multiple methods, the ENCODE TAF1 ChIP-seq data in H1 cells raises questions about whether TAF1 is truly absent or present at low levels. This uncertainty doesn't invalidate the core findings but suggests the absolute absence claim may be too strong.

The developmental model proposing that hESCs start with specialized TAF composition, transition to complete TFIID upon differentiation, then re-specialize in terminal differentiation is supported by the current data (R1, R2) combined with cited prior work on muscle and liver differentiation (C101, C102). This represents a conceptual advance over the previous progressive specialization model.
